summary: Describes how DNS SRV records can be used to find email submission and access services. It updates RFC 1939 and RFC 3501. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of guessing which computer handles your mail, your email program looks it up in the internet's phone book.

questions: how do mail clients discover servers with dns
how do mail clients find imap servers with dns
how does srv priority choose imap or pop3
what are the rfc 6186 srv service labels
subtitle: Mail programs can find a domain's mail servers from just an email address, using DNS SRV records.

tldr.problem: Mail programs usually make users type a server name and port for each mail service, which differs from program to program and leads to errors. Some programs instead probe a domain with a complex auto-discovery process.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SRV service labels for message submission, IMAP and POP3. A mail program takes the domain from the user's email address and looks up the matching SRV records to learn the server name and port.
tldr.outcome: A user only has to enter an email address. The priority field can also tell the program whether the domain prefers IMAP or POP3. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1939 and RFC 3501, and has itself been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 6186 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 1939 and RFC 3501, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8314 and RFC 8553.

sections.title: The Setup Problem
sections.content:
Email uses several protocols. SMTP moves mail, while IMAP and POP3 are message store access protocols that a message store user agent (MUA, a mail program) uses to work with mail after delivery. RFC 4409 defines a profile of SMTP just for message submission, and MUAs are expected to hand outgoing mail to a mail submission agent (MSA) that way.

Typically a user has had to type a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and port for each service. The RFC points out that this differs from one MUA to another and confuses users. Some MUAs instead probe a domain to see what is available, which the RFC calls a complex auto-discovery process.

The better approach is to ask the user for as little as possible: just their email address. RFC 2782 already defines DNS SRV resource records for locating services, and this RFC defines new SRV service types for submission, IMAP and POP3 so that MUAs can configure themselves.
sections.eli5: Setting up email used to mean typing in lots of tricky details. This RFC lets your email program work them out from just your email address.

sections.title: The SRV Service Labels
sections.content:
The RFC adds five service labels. submission identifies an MSA as defined in RFC 4409, and covers connections both with and without TLS.

For IMAP there are two labels. _imap names an IMAP server that MAY advertise LOGINDISABLED and MAY require the MUA to use STARTTLS before authenticating. _imaps names an IMAP server where TLS starts directly when the connection opens.

For POP3 the labels are _pop3, a server that MAY require the STLS command before authentication, and _pop3s, where TLS starts directly on connection.

The RFC gives example records such as _submission._tcp SRV 0 1 587 mail.example.com., _imap._tcp SRV 0 1 143 imap.example.com., _imaps._tcp SRV 0 1 993 imap.example.com., _pop3._tcp SRV 0 1 110 pop3.example.com. and _pop3s._tcp SRV 0 1 995 pop3.example.com.
sections.eli5: Each kind of mail service gets its own name tag in the phone book, with one tag for the plain version and one for the always-private version.

sections.title: Choosing Between IMAP and POP3
sections.content:
In an SRV record, a lower priority number means a higher preference. Sites often offer both IMAP and POP3 and may want to steer users toward one. Sites SHOULD publish both sets of records and give the preferred service the lower-numbered priority.

An MUA that supports both SHOULD fetch the records for both and use the service with the lowest priority value. If the priorities are equal, the MUA may choose either. If records for different protocols share a priority but have different weights, the client MUST first pick the protocol it intends to use, and only then run the weight selection algorithm from RFC 2782 on that protocol's records.

A service can be declared unavailable by setting the SRV target to .. Clients MUST then treat that service as not available and use the other records. In the RFC's last example the plain _imap and _pop3 records point at ., so only the TLS versions are offered, with IMAP at priority 0 preferred over POP3 at priority 10.
sections.eli5: The phone book can say "call this number first, and use that one only if you must". It can also say "this number does not exist here".

sections.title: What a Mail Program Does
sections.content:
The MUA asks only for the user's email address, splits it into local-part and domain, and uses the domain for SRV lookups. If a lookup succeeds, the target FQDN and port complete the configuration. If no SRV record exists, the MUA must ask the user for the details or use some other heuristic. When several records come back, the MUA MUST follow priority and weight as RFC 2782 describes.

On connecting, imaps and pop3s start a TLS negotiation immediately. With imap, pop3 and submission the commands STARTTLS, STLS and STARTTLS are used. MUAs SHOULD use TLS Server Name Indication, and certificate checks MUST follow Section 6 of RFC 6125, starting from the SRV record.

If a user identifier is needed, the MUA MUST first try the full email address, and SHOULD fall back to the local-part if that fails. If both fail, it SHOULD prompt the user.

After success, MUAs SHOULD cache the host name, port and user identity. If a later connection or login fails, they SHOULD repeat the SRV lookup, but MUST NOT switch between IMAP and POP3 because the priorities changed, unless the user is involved.
sections.eli5: Your mail program looks up your email's domain, calls the number it finds, and remembers it for next time. If it cannot find one, it just asks you.

sections.title: Rules for Service Providers
sections.content:
A provider that wants clients to configure themselves this way has three duties. First, IMAP, POP3 and submission servers SHOULD accept logins by either email address or email local-part. Addresses MUST NOT clash with other permitted login names, and local-parts need to be unique across the server and MUST NOT clash with any login name.

Second, if the provider uses TLS, it MUST install a certificate that MUAs can verify with the RFC 6125 procedure, starting from the SRV record. If several domains share one IP address, the provider MUST enable TLS Server Name Indication.

Third, the provider must install the appropriate SRV records for the services it offers.
sections.eli5: If you want your mail to be found this way, you must put your name in the phone book, let people sign in in either of two ways, and show a proper ID card.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a user has asked for a secure connection, the MUA MUST successfully negotiate transport layer security before sending any authentication command. Providers MAY offer any subset of the four options: imaps, pop3s, imap with STARTTLS, or pop3 with STLS.

An attacker who can alter DNS data, or get spoofed answers cached in a recursive resolver, could point an MUA at a server of the attacker's choosing. Without a secure DNS option, MUAs SHOULD check that the SRV target is in the domain that was queried, and otherwise SHOULD ask the user before connecting. Alternatively, when TLS is in use, MUAs MUST verify the service using Section 6 of RFC 6125.

Clients and servers MUST NOT request, offer or use SSL 2.0, because of known security vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: A trickster might scribble a wrong number in the phone book. So your mail program checks that the number looks right, and checks the other side's ID before it hands over your password.

data.title: SRV records with IMAP preferred
data.code:
_imap._tcp     SRV  0 0 0   .
_imaps._tcp    SRV  0 1 993 imap.example.com.
_pop3._tcp     SRV  0 0 0   .
_pop3s._tcp    SRV 10 1 995 pop3.example.com.
